test.title: Mini-test · The return of the night train

paragraphs.text: For several decades, overnight trains in Europe seemed to be disappearing. Cheap flights and high-speed daytime trains took their passengers, and many national rail companies closed their sleeper services because they lost money. By 2016, a traveller wishing to cross the continent overnight had far fewer choices than in the 1980s.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Since then, the trend has reversed. New routes have opened between major cities, and older services have been restored with modern carriages. Rail operators say demand has been driven largely by travellers who want to reduce the carbon emissions of their journeys, although many passengers also mention the convenience of travelling while they sleep and arriving in a city centre in the morning.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Running a night train is not simple. Sleeping carriages carry fewer passengers than seated ones, so each ticket must be more expensive, and the trains are used only once a day rather than several times. Crossing borders adds further complications, because operators must pay track charges in each country and meet different technical rules.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Prices remain the main obstacle for many travellers. A private cabin can cost more than a flight on the same route, although a place in a shared compartment is often competitive. Some governments have begun to offer subsidies, arguing that the environmental benefits justify public support, while critics reply that the money would do more good if spent on local transport.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Whether the revival lasts will depend on investment in new carriages, which take years to build, and on whether rail companies can agree on shared booking systems. At present, a passenger may need to use several different websites to book a single journey across three countries, a problem that operators have promised to solve.
paragraphs.label: E
